title: The Compose Race Your Coding Agent Inherits From You
summary:
Ask a coding agent for a Docker Compose file with Postgres, then cold-boot the result on a machine that has never run it. There is a good chance the app container starts, immediately asks for a database that does not exist yet, and fails its first connections. Wait a few seconds, try again, and everything works. The agent will tell you it tested the file. Both things are true, and the bug is older than the agent: it inherited the race from the tutorials it was trained on, and it also inherited the half-fix that looks like the fix.

Docker Compose is a tool for defining and running multi-container applications from one YAML file. I tested the generated shape, the half-fixed shape, and the corrected shape on my own host this week: three cold starts on fresh volumes (Docker Engine 29.1.3, Compose v5.1.4), the inherited race, the inherited half-fix that still races, and the three-line correction that actually holds. Everything below is from that run, with the run methodology and the timestamps as captured.

Key Takeaways

  • A bare depends_on: list only orders container startup. Compose explicitly does not wait for "ready", only "running" (Docker docs).
  • The most-copied Postgres healthcheck, pg_isready -U postgres, probes the Unix socket, and during first-boot initialization a temporary Postgres server answers on that socket before the real one is up (docker-library/postgres issue #146).
  • In my run, that socket-probe healthcheck reported the database healthy 4 seconds before Postgres actually accepted a TCP connection. The gate was wired correctly. The probe lied.
  • The fix is three edits: condition: service_healthy, restart: true, and -h 127.0.0.1 on the probe. My corrected file connected on attempt one, on a cold volume.

In this post:

  • Why does the race survive a working demo?

  • Why doesn't the copied healthcheck fix it?
  • What does the fixed file look like?
  • How do you review agent YAML in 60 seconds?

What does the agent actually write?

Two lines date a compose file, and agents write both of them together.

The first is the bare dependency list. In the long form of depends_on, per the compose-file services reference, this same key takes a condition instead, which is the part the 2021 corpus never learned:

services:
  app:
    depends_on:
      - db

The second is the socket-probe healthcheck on the database. healthcheck is a container configuration that makes the runtime probe the service at a fixed interval and report a health status:

  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]

Neither line is broken on its own. The first one does exactly what it says: start db before app. The second one does exactly what it says: exit 0 when something answers on the Postgres Unix socket. The problem is what they don't say, and they cluster in generated files because they cluster in the training corpus. Both come from the same generation of quick-start guides, the ones that shipped years before the long-form depends_on with conditions was common knowledge.

The evidence that this is a corpus problem, not a reasoning problem, is now measured. Work on updating model knowledge after API changes found that models continue generating outdated API calls "even with access to current documentation" (arXiv:2506.20495). A study of deprecated-API recommendations reports that 37.4 percent of GPT-3.5's API predictions were deprecated, and that fixing this by retraining is impractical because library APIs change too fast (arXiv:2511.21022). Compose YAML is not a Python library call, but the mechanism transfers exactly: the spec moved, the tutorials didn't, and the average of the corpus is the 2021 shape.

Why does the race survive a working demo?

Because a warm volume hides it.

Postgres only does its slow first-boot work when the data directory is empty. The entrypoint script runs initdb, starts a temporary server for the setup phase, runs anything mounted in /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/, and only then hands over to the real server as PID 1. On a volume that has already been initialized, the container skips all of that, and the gap between "container running" and "accepting connections" shrinks to near zero. Whoever verifies the compose file, human or agent, usually verifies it on a warm volume. The demo passes. The agent's confidence is not fake; the test genuinely passed on the machine it had.

The first cold start is the one that pays for it: CI runner, teammate's laptop, fresh VM. That is the boot where the app container starts a beat after the database container and asks a half-initialized Postgres for a connection.

Here is the output of that exact cold start from my run, an alpine app probing db:5432 every half second in a loop. Consider it the shape of every "it works on the second try" bug report you have ever closed:

app-1  | ATTEMPT 1: CONNECTION-REFUSED
app-1  | ATTEMPT 2: CONNECTION-REFUSED
app-1  | ATTEMPT 3: CONNECTION-REFUSED
app-1  | ATTEMPT 4: CONNECTION-REFUSED
app-1  | ATTEMPT 5: CONNECTED

Two seconds of refused connections on a fast local disk. The database log tells you why: the "ready to accept connections" line lands at 08:10:28, after the app has already been asking. On a slower disk, or with init scripts in /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/, the window stretches to seconds more. If your app has restart: unless-stopped, Compose quietly restarts it until it sticks, the stack comes up, and the race is invisible again until the morning it crash-loops.

I documented the anatomy of this race in the healthcheck deep-dive earlier in this series. The part that is new here is where the YAML came from, and the fact that the obvious fix, asking the agent to add a healthcheck, often doesn't fix it.

What did I actually run?

Three cold starts on my own host: Docker Engine 29.1.3, Docker Compose v5.1.4, with alpine:3.20 as the app and postgres:16-alpine as the database. Every run started from a deleted volume, so Postgres went through its full first-boot initialization each time. The app is deliberately dumb, a shell loop that tries db:5432 every half second and prints the result, so the timing is visible and nothing else can mask it:

services:
  app:
    image: alpine:3.20
    depends_on:
      - db
    command: >
      sh -c 'i=0;
      while [ $$i -lt 30 ]; do
        i=$$((i+1));
        if nc -z -w 1 db 5432 2>/dev/null; then
          echo "ATTEMPT $$i: CONNECTED";
          exit 0;
        else
          echo "ATTEMPT $$i: CONNECTION-REFUSED";
        fi;
        sleep 0.5;
      done;
      echo "GAVE UP"'

For the third run, to make the initialization window wide enough to observe, I mounted a one-line init script into /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/ that sleeps four seconds. The sleep does not create the gap, it only stretches the same initialization phase that already existed in the first run, and every timestamp below comes from docker inspect and the Postgres log, not from my watch. The three runs, all from the same host:

Run File shape Outcome
1 bare depends_on list 4 refused connections, connected on attempt 5
2 service_healthy + TCP probe connected on attempt 1, app held until Healthy
3 service_healthy + socket probe "healthy" 4s early, 7 refused connections after the verdict

Why doesn't the copied healthcheck fix it?

Here is where the inherited fix becomes worse than the inherited race. Ask an agent to fix the startup race and it will, correctly, reach for the long-form dependency. service_healthy is the depends_on condition that holds the dependent container back until the dependency's healthcheck reports healthy:

  app:
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy

That is the right gate. Compose will not start the app until the database's healthcheck reports healthy. But the healthcheck it copies, the same one from the same tutorials, is pg_isready -U postgres, and pg_isready without a host flag connects to the Unix socket. pg_isready is the Postgres client's readiness probe; it exits 0 when a server accepts connections. On the official Postgres image, first boot runs a temporary server for initialization that listens on the Unix socket only. The probe passes while the real server, the one your app connects to over TCP, is not up yet. The maintainers have been explaining this in issue #146 for years: "Simply adding -h 127.0.0.1 to the pg_isready command line should be enough to detect readiness correctly."

I ran that combination, the correct gate with the copied probe, and watched docker inspect while it happened. The healthcheck went starting at +0.78 seconds and healthy at +3.02 seconds. The real server accepted its first TCP connection at +7.06 seconds. Four seconds of lie. Compose trusted the verdict, started the app, and the app did this:

app-1  | ATTEMPT 1: CONNECTION-REFUSED
app-1  | ATTEMPT 2: CONNECTION-REFUSED
app-1  | ATTEMPT 3: CONNECTION-REFUSED
app-1  | ATTEMPT 4: CONNECTION-REFUSED
app-1  | ATTEMPT 5: CONNECTION-REFUSED
app-1  | ATTEMPT 6: CONNECTION-REFUSED
app-1  | ATTEMPT 7: CONNECTION-REFUSED
app-1  | ATTEMPT 8: CONNECTED

Seven refused connections after the container was declared healthy. The probe log shows the mechanics, and it is worth reading slowly because it is the whole post in three lines:

08:13:52.4  exit 0  /var/run/postgresql:5432 - accepting connections
08:13:54.5  exit 0  /var/run/postgresql:5432 - accepting connections
08:13:56.5  exit 2  /var/run/postgresql:5432 - no response

The first two probes passed against the temporary initialization server, on the socket. Then the entrypoint shut that server down to finish init work, and the third probe failed, no response, while the real server was still seconds away. The status even flipped to unhealthy for a moment during the handoff. If the failure had landed one probe later, after the container was already marked healthy, the streak would have needed three consecutive failures to matter, and by then the app had long since started and crashed.

This is the failure mode that makes people conclude the healthcheck pattern "doesn't work" and delete it. The gate worked. The probe answered a different question than the one the app asks.

What does the fixed file look like?

Three edits to the generated file, and my run 2 output after them:

 Container racefix-db-1  Started
 Container racefix-db-1  Waiting
 Container racefix-db-1  Healthy
 Container racefix-app-1 Starting
 Container racefix-app-1 Started
app-1  | ATTEMPT 1: CONNECTED

The app is not created until db reports Healthy, and its very first connection lands. The full file:

services:
  app:
    image: alpine:3.20
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
        restart: true
    command: >
      sh -c 'i=0;
      while [ $$i -lt 30 ]; do
        i=$$((i+1));
        if nc -z -w 1 db 5432 2>/dev/null; then
          echo "ATTEMPT $$i: CONNECTED";
          exit 0;
        else
          echo "ATTEMPT $$i: CONNECTION-REFUSED";
        fi;
        sleep 0.5;
      done;
      echo "GAVE UP"'

  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: example
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -h 127.0.0.1 -U postgres"]
      interval: 2s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10
      start_period: 10s

volumes:
  pgdata:

The three edits, one line each. condition: service_healthy makes Compose wait for the healthcheck verdict instead of container start, the gate. restart: true re-runs that gate when you explicitly restart the database, so the app is not left pointing at stale connections after a docker compose restart db. And -h 127.0.0.1 forces the probe onto TCP, where the temporary initialization server cannot answer it, the honest probe. The timing knobs around it matter too, start_period especially: they give a slow first boot room to finish before failures start counting. On a cold volume my database needed about seven seconds, so 10 seconds of grace is the floor I would ship, and CI on shared runners gets more.

Keep the application-side retry anyway. The gate protects the startup sequence only. If Postgres restarts two hours later, nothing re-runs the gate for you, a limit I pushed on in the exit-0 OOM post from the other angle: a green healthcheck reports its own probe, not your app's reality.

How do you review agent YAML in 60 seconds?

You do not need to run the stack to catch this class of bug. Read the diff against the current spec, the same way you would review a human's PR.

Check the dependency wiring first. A bare depends_on: - db list means no waiting; it needs the long form with condition: service_healthy to gate startup. Check the probe next, because this is the part everyone trusts. pg_isready with no -h flag is a socket probe; on the Postgres image that can pass during initialization. It needs -h 127.0.0.1 (or the service name, if you want the probe to mirror app traffic) to test the path your app actually uses. Check the timing budget after that: no start_period means a slow first boot spends its failure budget before the database had a chance. CI runners are slower than your laptop, so give the budget headroom there. And check what happens after startup: no restart: true on the dependency means a deliberate database restart leaves the app on stale connections.

Then fix the input, not just the output. The prompt that produces current YAML is a prompt with current references in it. Paste the startup-order doc and the services reference links into the request, and say "gate the app on service_healthy with a TCP probe" instead of "write me a compose file with Postgres". The model still carries the old corpus, and it will still try the 2021 shape when you let it guess. But it does not argue with a pasted spec. The measured version of this instinct is the ReCode result: outdated API knowledge persists "even with access to current documentation" (arXiv:2506.20495). The documentation you paste is doing real work, and the review pass you run after is doing the rest.

One more habit that pays for itself: cold-boot the result before you merge it. On a scratch project, docker compose down -v && docker compose up --wait is a 30-second test. It reproduces exactly the run that fails in CI, and --wait turns the healthcheck into the pass/fail signal instead of a grepped log line.

FAQ

Doesn't restart: unless-stopped already handle this?
It hides it. The app crash-loops until the database happens to be ready, then looks healthy. The race is still there; you just stopped being able to see it.

Does the long depends_on form without condition wait for readiness?
No. Without condition: service_healthy it is equivalent to the short list: ordering only.

Is docker compose up --wait enough for CI?
Yes, and it is the right tool: it blocks until healthchecked services report healthy. It does not remove the need for the gate on the app service itself, or for an honest probe.

Do I still need app-level retries if the gate works?
Yes. The gate runs at startup only. A connection that drops an hour later is the application's problem, and the same retry-with-backoff loop you already write for production networks covers it.

Where does this leave the agent?

The agent is not wrong that the file works. It worked on the machine it had, with the volume it had, and the corpus it was trained on says that file is what a compose file looks like. The spec moved, the tutorials didn't, and the average of all that 2021 YAML is what comes out when you ask for 2026 infrastructure. The three-line diff between the inherited shape and the current one is small, it is mechanical, and it is exactly the kind of review you were going to do anyway on a file nobody typed by hand.

What is the oldest line of config an agent has handed you that you only caught because it failed somewhere strange? I am collecting these for a follow-up, and the comments are where I will read them.

Claims about model behavior are cited to the linked papers, and anything I could not reproduce myself is not in this post.

The measured version of this instinct is the ReCode result: outdated API knowledge persists "even with access to current documentation" (arXiv:2506.20495). The documentation you paste is doing real work, and the review pass you run after is doing the rest.

One more habit that pays for itself: cold-boot the result before you merge it. On a scratch project, docker compose down -v && docker compose up --wait is a 30-second test. It reproduces exactly the run that fails in CI, and --wait turns the healthcheck into the pass/fail signal instead of a grepped log line.

FAQ

Doesn't restart: unless-stopped already handle this?
It hides it. The app crash-loops until the database happens to be ready, then looks healthy. The race is still there; you just stopped being able to see it.

Does the long depends_on form without condition wait for readiness?
No. Without condition: service_healthy it is equivalent to the short list: ordering only.

Is docker compose up --wait enough for CI?
Yes, and it is the right tool: it blocks until healthchecked services report healthy. It does not remove the need for the gate on the app service itself, or for an honest probe.

Do I still need app-level retries if the gate works?
Yes. The gate runs at startup only. A connection that drops an hour later is the application's problem, and the same retry-with-backoff loop you already write for production networks covers it.

Where does this leave the agent?

The agent is not wrong that the file works. It worked on the machine it had, with the volume it had, and the corpus it was trained on says that file is what a compose file looks like. The spec moved, the tutorials didn't, and the average of all that 2021 YAML is what comes out when you ask for 2026 infrastructure. The three-line diff between the inherited shape and the current one is small, it is mechanical, and it is exactly the kind of review you were going to do anyway on a file nobody typed by hand.

What is the oldest line of config an agent has handed you that you only caught because it failed somewhere strange? I am collecting these for a follow-up, and the comments are where I will read them.

Verified against Docker Engine 29.1.3 and Docker Compose v5.1.4 on 2026-10-29, with three cold-start runs on fresh volumes; every timestamp and probe result above is from docker inspect or the Postgres log of those runs. Claims about model behavior are cited to the linked papers, and anything I could not reproduce myself is not in this post.

Sources

Every claim above traces to these primary sources. Where I could not verify something hands-on, the post says so.

  • Diagram artwork: dated tutorial books flow into a glowing model core that outputs a compose file card

title: The Site Moved. The Scheduler Didn't: 19 Days of Silent Background Jobs After a Migration
summary:
We moved a busy local news site to a new server. The migration checklist was long and we were proud of it: files, database, media, DNS, TLS, redirects, image paths, mail, a performance pass. The home page loaded in half a second instead of four. Editors logged in, wrote stories, and published them. Every check we had was green.

Nineteen days later, during a routine look at table sizes, one number stood out. A small table that normally holds a few thousand rows had close to 600,000. Nothing was broken from the outside. The site was fast, pages returned 200, nobody had complained.

The table was big because the job that trims it had not run once since the migration. Neither had any other background job. The application's scheduler, a single crontab line, had never been added on the new server.

This post is about why that kind of failure is invisible, what it actually cost us, and the three checks we now treat as part of every move.

How the scheduler works in this application

The CMS has one scheduler entry point. The operating system runs it every minute from cron:

* * * * * /path/to/php /path/to/app/scheduler.php > /dev/null 2>&1

That one script reads a list of jobs from the database, each with its own interval, and runs whichever are due. The list is long: publishing posts that were scheduled for a future time, rolling raw visit logs up into hourly statistics, deleting old rows from logging and rate-limit tables, rebuilding sitemaps, refreshing small data widgets, sending queued notifications.

This design is convenient. Adding a job is a database row, not a server change. It is also a single point of failure that lives outside the application's code, in the system crontab of whatever user the site runs as. Copy the files and the database, and you have copied the job list but not the thing that runs it.

Why nobody noticed for 19 days

Look at what each job does and ask who would see it fail.

  • Scheduled publishing. Editors who schedule a story for 06:00 would notice when it doesn't appear. On this site the newsroom publishes immediately; nobody had scheduled anything. We checked afterwards: no posts were stuck in a scheduled state.
  • Statistics roll-up. The admin dashboard reads today's numbers from the raw log, so "today" looked fine. Only longer ranges, built from the hourly summaries, were going stale, and nobody had opened a monthly report yet.
  • Cleanup jobs. Their whole effect is that something doesn't happen: a table doesn't grow. A table that is growing gives no signal until it is big enough to slow a query or fill a disk.
  • Data widgets. Currency rates, weather and football fixtures were the only visibly stale things. We had actually noticed those during the migration and fixed them by adding a few dedicated cron lines, one per widget. That fix made the problem harder to see: the visible symptoms went away, so the missing scheduler line looked like it had been handled.

Our uptime monitor checked the home page and an article page. Both were fine. A health check that only asks "does the page render" will never see a job that didn't run, because the page doesn't depend on it today.

There is a general rule hiding here: the failure of a background job is invisible until the job's absence becomes a foreground problem. Cleanup jobs take weeks. Aggregation jobs take until someone opens a report. Publishing jobs take until someone schedules a post.

What it cost

In this case, less than it could have. No content was lost and nothing went down. The damage was:

  • A rate-limit and request log table with roughly 594,000 rows that should have held a few days of data. Inserts into it happen on every request, so it was slowly making every request a little more expensive.
  • Nineteen days without hourly statistics summaries. Summaries can only be rebuilt from raw logs that still exist. Here the raw logs were still there, because the cleanup hadn't run either. If the roll-up had stopped while the cleanup kept running, the raw data behind those reports would have been deleted on schedule.
  • A few days of security log retention that was longer than our own policy says it should be.

The more uncomfortable cost is what would have happened on a different site. On a site that relies on scheduled publishing, the morning's stories would have stayed drafts, and the newsroom would have discovered it at 06:01 on a weekday.

The fix itself was one line 

crontab -u siteuser -l > crontab-before.txt   # keep the old state
( crontab -u siteuser -l 2>/dev/null; \
  echo '* * * * * /path/to/php -d date.timezone=Europe/Istanbul /path/to/app/scheduler.php > /dev/null 2>&1' \
) | crontab -u siteuser -

Two details mattered more than the line:

  1. The per-widget lines had to go. They were now duplicates of jobs the scheduler also runs. Two copies of the same job, running at slightly different times, is its own source of subtle bugs.
  2. The site sat behind a CDN proxy, and some jobs call the site's own URLs. From the server, those requests went out to the CDN and back in, picking up rate limits and bot checks on the way. Pointing the site's own hostnames at the local machine in /etc/hosts keeps self-requests local.

Before turning the scheduler on, we checked for posts with a publish time in the past that were still waiting. A scheduler that has been off for weeks will publish all of them in its first minute. On a migrated site those can be old test posts, so look before you enable.

After enabling it, the job table told us within two minutes whether it worked:

SELECT name, last_run, last_status
FROM scheduled_jobs
ORDER BY last_run DESC
LIMIT 10;

The jobs started showing fresh last_run values, and the oversized table was left to the regular nightly cleanup instead of a manual DELETE during business hours.

Three checks we now run on every migration

1. Diff the crontabs, not just the files

Before the move, dump every crontab that touches the site: the site user's, root's, and any system cron file that mentions the site's path.

crontab -u siteuser -l
crontab -l | grep -F '/path/to/app'
grep -rlF '/path/to/app' /etc/cron.d /etc/crontab 2>/dev/null

After the move, run the same commands on the new server and compare. Any line that exists on the old server and not the new one is either a deliberate decision, written down, or a bug. We had migrated the files with rsync, the database with a dump, and the crontab with memory. Memory lost.

2. Monitor "time since last run", not "is the site up"

The scheduler already wrote a last_run timestamp for every job. Nothing was reading it. We added a check to our regular server health script that asks one question per site:

SELECT COUNT(*) AS stale
FROM scheduled_jobs
WHERE enabled = 1
  AND last_run < NOW() - INTERVAL 10 MINUTE
  AND run_every_minutes <= 5;

If a job that should run every few minutes has not run in ten, the check warns. It also warns if the site has no scheduler line in any crontab at all. This turns an invisible failure into a visible one within minutes instead of weeks.

If your application doesn't record job runs, the cheapest version is a heartbeat: have the scheduler touch a file or ping a URL every run, and alert when the file's age passes a threshold. Dead-man's-switch services exist for exactly this, and a ten-line script against a timestamp does the same job.

3. Put the scheduler in the definition of "migrated"

Our checklist said "copy cron jobs" somewhere in the middle. It now says, as the last step before anyone signs off:

The scheduler is running on the new server. Proof: the job table shows a last_run within the last two minutes for every enabled job.

A checklist item that needs a timestamp as evidence is hard to tick by accident. "Copy cron jobs" was easy to tick after adding the six widget lines, because cron jobs had, in fact, been copied.

What to take from this

  • A scheduler that lives in the system crontab is part of your deployment, even if every job it runs lives in your database.
  • Background job failures are silent by design. Plan for that by monitoring their timestamps, because their effects will show up late and somewhere else.
  • When you fix a symptom during a migration, ask what produced it. We fixed stale widgets one by one and missed that they all had the same cause.
  • Before re-enabling a scheduler that has been off, look at the queue it will process. Days of backlog can run in one minute.

We run a small fleet of news sites on the same CMS at Alesta WEB, and the stale-job check now runs against all of them as part of regular server maintenance. It is a few lines of SQL, and it would have caught this on day one.

title: Moving a production API to Hetzner, part 2: hardening and configuring the server
summary:
Series: Part 1: choosing and creating the server · Part 2: hardening and configuring it · Part 3: migrating data and cutting over

In part 1 we created a Hetzner CX23 behind a Cloud Firewall, with a
cloud-init config meant to harden it on first boot. This part does that hardening
by hand, one step at a time, explains every line, and does it without ever
risking a lockout.

(cloud-init is the tool in every cloud image that runs once on first boot and
applies the config you paste into the Cloud config box: users, files,
packages, commands. Part 1, section 5 has the full config and how it works.)

Why by hand, if cloud-init can do it?

  • You'll know what each setting does, so you can debug it when it misbehaves.
  • It works anywhere: on a provider without cloud-init, on a server someone else created, or when cloud-init failed or was never given its config.
  • It doubles as the verification. If you did use cloud-init, skip to section 5 ("Verify like an attacker") and run the checks. They prove the config was applied, not just pasted.

Placeholders, as before: the new server is 198.51.100.20 and the old one is
203.0.113.10.

1. ~/.ssh/config: two servers, two keys, short commands

The problem it solves

During a migration you constantly talk to two machines, each with its own
address, port and key. Typing
ssh -p 2222 -i ~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519 ubuntu@198.51.100.20 every time is slow
and error-prone. ~/.ssh/config gives each server a short name:

Host old-box
  HostName 203.0.113.10
  Port 2222
  User ubuntu
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/oldhost_key.pem
  IdentitiesOnly yes

Host new-box
  HostName 198.51.100.20
  Port 2222
  User ubuntu
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519
  IdentitiesOnly yes

Now ssh new-box means all of that. So do scp file new-box:, rsync … new-box:,
and git clone new-box:…. Every OpenSSH-based tool reads this file.

You can append a block without opening an editor:

printf '\nHost new-box\n  HostName 198.51.100.20\n  Port 2222\n  User ubuntu\n  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519\n  IdentitiesOnly yes\n' >> ~/.ssh/config

Why IdentitiesOnly yes

Without it, the client offers the server every key in your ssh-agent, one by
one, before the one you named. sshd allows only a few attempts per connection
(MaxAuthTries, default 6). With enough keys loaded you get
Too many authentication failures before the right key is ever tried.
IdentitiesOnly yes means "offer only the IdentityFile named here". It also
stops you from accidentally presenting your work key to a personal server.

2. First login, and the plan for not locking yourself out

On a stock Hetzner image, before any hardening, there is exactly one account you
can reach: root, on port 22, with the SSH key you selected at creation.
Hetzner writes that key into /root/.ssh/authorized_keys and sets no root
password. So that's where we start:

ssh -p 22 -i ~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519 -o IdentitiesOnly=yes root@198.51.100.20 'id; ss -tln'

(If cloud-init did run, root login is already disabled and this is refused. That's
your cue to skip to the checks in section 5.)

What happened to me: I created the server and forgot to paste the cloud
config. My first ssh -p 2222 got Connection refused, because nothing was
listening on 2222 (section 6 explains how to read that). Recreating the server
would have meant giving up a CX23 that was close to sold out, so I hardened it
by hand, as below.

Running a command after the host ('id; ss -tln') executes it remotely and
returns. No interactive shell is needed, which makes every step repeatable and
easy to paste into notes.

The lockout problem

Hardening SSH means changing the very thing you're connected through. Get one
line wrong, for example disabling root before the new user's key works, and the
next connection fails. On a cloud server, your remaining way in is the provider's
web console. Remember from part 1 that Hetzner sets no root password when you
use an SSH key, so even the console needs a password reset first.

The fix is to make changes in two passes, with a test in between, so that at
every moment at least one known-good way in still works:

3. Pass 1, explained block by block

The whole pass is one script, sent from the laptop and run on the server as root.
'bash -s' tells the remote bash to read its script from standard input, and the
heredoc (<<'EOF' … EOF) supplies it. The quotes around 'EOF' stop your
local shell from expanding $variables inside, so they reach the server as
written.

ssh -p 22 -i ~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519 -o IdentitiesOnly=yes root@198.51.100.20 'bash -s' <<'EOF'
set -euo pipefail
export DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive

# --- user ---
id ubuntu >/dev/null 2>&1 || adduser --disabled-password --gecos "" ubuntu
usermod -aG sudo ubuntu
echo 'ubuntu ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL' > /etc/sudoers.d/90-ubuntu && chmod 440 /etc/sudoers.d/90-ubuntu
install -d -m 700 -o ubuntu -g ubuntu /home/ubuntu/.ssh
install -m 600 -o ubuntu -g ubuntu /root/.ssh/authorized_keys /home/ubuntu/.ssh/authorized_keys

# --- packages ---
apt-get update -q
apt-get -y -q -o Dpkg::Options::=--force-confold upgrade
apt-get -y -q install ufw unattended-upgrades

# --- sshd ---
cat > /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-hardening.conf <<'CONF'
Port 22
Port 2222
PasswordAuthentication no
KbdInteractiveAuthentication no
PermitRootLogin prohibit-password
PubkeyAuthentication yes
CONF
sshd -t
systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl restart ssh.socket || true
systemctl restart ssh || true

# --- docker log rotation (read when Docker is installed later) ---
mkdir -p /etc/docker
echo '{"log-driver": "json-file", "log-opts": {"max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3"}}' > /etc/docker/daemon.json

# --- host firewall ---
ufw default deny incoming; ufw default allow outgoing
for r in 22/tcp 2222/tcp 80/tcp 443/tcp 443/udp; do ufw allow $r; done
ufw --force enable

# --- swap ---
if [ ! -f /swapfile ]; then fallocate -l 2G /swapfile && chmod 600 /swapfile && mkswap /swapfile && swapon /swapfile && echo '/swapfile none swap sw 0 0' >> /etc/fstab; fi

ss -tln | grep -E ":(22|2222) "
EOF

set -euo pipefail

These are bash's "fail loudly" settings: -e stops at the first failing command,
-u treats an unset variable as an error, and pipefail makes a pipeline fail
if any stage fails, not just the last. Part 3 shows pipefail biting back,
too.

The user

  • adduser --disabled-password: the account has no password at all, so it can only be reached with a key. id ubuntu || … makes the line safe to run twice.
  • sudoers.d/90-ubuntu with NOPASSWD: ubuntu can run sudo without a password, which is what Ubuntu cloud images give their default user. It's a trade-off: if someone gets this account they get root. But a password-less account with a sudo password needs a password set somewhere, and that's a secret to manage. With key-only SSH, the key is the boundary. chmod 440 because sudo refuses sudoers files that others can write to.
  • install -d -m 700 / install -m 600: create .ssh and copy root's authorized_keys with the right owner and permissions in one step. The permissions aren't cosmetic. sshd's StrictModes (on by default) ignores an authorized_keys file that other users could modify, and the symptom is a baffling Permission denied (publickey).

Packages

DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive and --force-confold stop apt from opening an
interactive "a config file changed, which version do you want?" prompt in the
middle of a non-interactive SSH session. confold keeps the existing file.

sshd: drop-in files and "first value wins"

Instead of editing /etc/ssh/sshd_config, we add a file in
/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/. The main config includes that directory near its
top, and the files load in name order. For most settings sshd keeps the
first value it reads, so 10-hardening.conf beats the image's own
50-cloud-init.conf and anything below in the main file. Package upgrades never
touch your drop-in, either.

Line Meaning
Port 22, Port 2222 listen on both (repeatable directive)
PasswordAuthentication no no password logins, so bots guessing passwords get nowhere
KbdInteractiveAuthentication no closes the other password path (PAM "keyboard-interactive"), which can otherwise ask for a password even with the line above
PermitRootLogin prohibit-password pass 1 only: root may log in with a key, our safety line. Pass 2 changes it to no
PubkeyAuthentication yes keys, explicitly

Two commands make it safe:

  • sshd -t tests the configuration and exits non-zero on a syntax error. Because of set -e, a typo stops the script before the restart, so the old, working sshd keeps running.
  • sshd -T (used later) prints the effective configuration after all files are merged. That's the only reliable way to know which value won.

Why ssh.socket and not just ssh

Since Ubuntu 24.04, sshd is socket-activated: systemd holds the listening
socket (ssh.socket) and starts sshd when a connection arrives. Which ports that
socket listens on is generated from sshd_config by a systemd generator, and
the generator only runs on systemctl daemon-reload. So changing Port takes
three steps: reload (regenerate the socket), restart ssh.socket (rebind the
ports), restart ssh. Skip the reload and sshd's config says 2222 while nothing
listens there. || true keeps the script going on releases that aren't
socket-activated.

The script ends by printing what's listening. We got
0.0.0.0:22, 0.0.0.0:2222, [::]:22 and [::]:2222.

ufw: the host firewall

ufw ("uncomplicated firewall") is a front end for the kernel's netfilter
(nftables). Default deny incoming and allow outgoing, then open exactly
what's needed. 22 is allowed before ufw enable, otherwise enabling it would
cut the very session doing the enabling.

Docker bypasses ufw for published ports (see part 1), so ufw protects sshd and
anything else running directly on the host, and the Cloud Firewall protects
everything. Two layers, each covering the other's blind spot. That's
defence in depth.

Swap

A 4 GB server with no swap handles a memory spike (a big query, a container
starting) by invoking the kernel's OOM killer, which usually kills the biggest
process: Postgres. A 2 GB swapfile turns that crash into a brief slowdown.
fallocate reserves the space instantly, mkswap formats it, swapon activates
it, and the /etc/fstab line brings it back after a reboot.

4. Test, then pass 2

Before taking anything away, prove the new way in works:

ssh new-box 'whoami; sudo -n true && echo sudo-ok'

ubuntu
sudo-ok

sudo -n means "non-interactive": fail instead of prompting. So this proves
both the key and passwordless sudo. Only now, as ubuntu, turn root off:

ssh new-box 'sudo sed -i "s/^PermitRootLogin .*/PermitRootLogin no/" /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-hardening.conf && sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl restart ssh && sudo sshd -T | grep -E "^(port|permitrootlogin|passwordauthentication) "'

port 22
port 2222
permitrootlogin no
passwordauthentication no

5. Verify like an attacker

Checking the config proves what you intended. Negative tests prove what's

ssh -p 2222 -i ~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519 -o IdentitiesOnly=yes root@198.51.100.20 true
# root@198.51.100.20: Permission denied (publickey).

ssh -p 2222 -o PubkeyAuthentication=no -o PreferredAuthentications=password ubuntu@198.51.100.20 true
# ubuntu@198.51.100.20: Permission denied (publickey).

The second line is the interesting one. We asked for password authentication,
and the server's reply lists only (publickey) as acceptable. It doesn't offer
a password prompt at all.

Then the rest of the configuration in one go:

ssh new-box 'sudo ufw status verbose; ss -tln; timedatectl show -p NTPSynchronized; swapon --show; free -h; df -h /; cat /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/20auto-upgrades; systemctl is-enabled unattended-upgrades; ls /var/run/reboot-required 2>/dev/null && echo REBOOT-NEEDED'

event_model_payload.summary:
Series: Part 1: choosing and creating the server · Part 2: hardening and configuring it · Part 3: migrating data and cutting over

In part 1 we created a Hetzner CX23 behind a Cloud Firewall, with a
cloud-init config meant to harden it on first boot. This part does that hardening
by hand, one step at a time, explains every line, and does it without ever
risking a lockout.

(cloud-init is the tool in every cloud image that runs once on first boot and
applies the config you paste into the Cloud config box: users, files,
packages, commands. Part 1, section 5 has the full config and how it works.)

Why by hand, if cloud-init can do it?

  • You'll know what each setting does, so you can debug it when it misbehaves.
  • It works anywhere: on a provider without cloud-init, on a server someone else created, or when cloud-init failed or was never given its config.
  • It doubles as the verification. If you did use cloud-init, skip to section 5 ("Verify like an attacker") and run the checks. They prove the config was applied, not just pasted.

Placeholders, as before: the new server is 198.51.100.20 and the old one is
203.0.113.10.

1. ~/.ssh/config: two servers, two keys, short commands

The problem it solves

During a migration you constantly talk to two machines, each with its own
address, port and key. Typing
ssh -p 2222 -i ~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519 ubuntu@198.51.100.20 every time is slow
and error-prone. ~/.ssh/config gives each server a short name:

Host old-box
  HostName 203.0.113.10
  Port 2222
  User ubuntu
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/oldhost_key.pem
  IdentitiesOnly yes

Host new-box
  HostName 198.51.100.20
  Port 2222
  User ubuntu
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519
  IdentitiesOnly yes

Now ssh new-box means all of that. So do scp file new-box:, rsync … new-box:,
and git clone new-box:…. Every OpenSSH-based tool reads this file.

You can append a block without opening an editor:

printf '\nHost new-box\n  HostName 198.51.100.20\n  Port 2222\n  User ubuntu\n  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519\n  IdentitiesOnly yes\n' >> ~/.ssh/config

Why IdentitiesOnly yes

Without it, the client offers the server every key in your ssh-agent, one by
one, before the one you named. sshd allows only a few attempts per connection
(MaxAuthTries, default 6). With enough keys loaded you get
Too many authentication failures before the right key is ever tried.
IdentitiesOnly yes means "offer only the IdentityFile named here". It also
stops you from accidentally presenting your work key to a personal server.

2. First login, and the plan for not locking yourself out

On a stock Hetzner image, before any hardening, there is exactly one account you
can reach: root, on port 22, with the SSH key you selected at creation.
Hetzner writes that key into /root/.ssh/authorized_keys and sets no root
password. So that's where we start:

ssh -p 22 -i ~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519 -o IdentitiesOnly=yes root@198.51.100.20 'id; ss -tln'

(If cloud-init did run, root login is already disabled and this is refused. That's
your cue to skip to the checks in section 5.)

config. My first ssh -p 2222 got Connection refused, because nothing was
listening on 2222 (section 6 explains how to read that). Recreating the server
would have meant giving up a CX23 that was close to sold out, so I hardened it
by hand, as below.

Running a command after the host ('id; ss -tln') executes it remotely and
returns. No interactive shell is needed, which makes every step repeatable and
easy to paste into notes.

The lockout problem

Hardening SSH means changing the very thing you're connected through. Get one
line wrong, for example disabling root before the new user's key works, and the
next connection fails. On a cloud server, your remaining way in is the provider's
web console. Remember from part 1 that Hetzner sets no root password when you
use an SSH key, so even the console needs a password reset first.

The fix is to make changes in two passes, with a test in between, so that at
every moment at least one known-good way in still works:

3. Pass 1, explained block by block

The whole pass is one script, sent from the laptop and run on the server as root.
'bash -s' tells the remote bash to read its script from standard input, and the
heredoc (<<'EOF' … EOF) supplies it. The quotes around 'EOF' stop your
local shell from expanding $variables inside, so they reach the server as
written.

ssh -p 22 -i ~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519 -o IdentitiesOnly=yes root@198.51.100.20 'bash -s' <<'EOF'
set -euo pipefail
export DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive

# --- user ---
id ubuntu >/dev/null 2>&1 || adduser --disabled-password --gecos "" ubuntu
usermod -aG sudo ubuntu
echo 'ubuntu ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL' > /etc/sudoers.d/90-ubuntu && chmod 440 /etc/sudoers.d/90-ubuntu
install -d -m 700 -o ubuntu -g ubuntu /home/ubuntu/.ssh
install -m 600 -o ubuntu -g ubuntu /root/.ssh/authorized_keys /home/ubuntu/.ssh/authorized_keys

# --- packages ---
apt-get update -q
apt-get -y -q -o Dpkg::Options::=--force-confold upgrade
apt-get -y -q install ufw unattended-upgrades

# --- sshd ---
cat > /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-hardening.conf <<'CONF'
Port 22
Port 2222
PasswordAuthentication no
KbdInteractiveAuthentication no
PermitRootLogin prohibit-password
PubkeyAuthentication yes
CONF
sshd -t
systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl restart ssh.socket || true
systemctl restart ssh || true

# --- docker log rotation (read when Docker is installed later) ---
mkdir -p /etc/docker
echo '{"log-driver": "json-file", "log-opts": {"max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3"}}' > /etc/docker/daemon.json

# --- host firewall ---
ufw default deny incoming; ufw default allow outgoing
for r in 22/tcp 2222/tcp 80/tcp 443/tcp 443/udp; do ufw allow $r; done
ufw --force enable

# --- swap ---
if [ ! -f /swapfile ]; then fallocate -l 2G /swapfile && chmod 600 /swapfile && mkswap /swapfile && swapon /swapfile && echo '/swapfile none swap sw 0 0' >> /etc/fstab; fi

ss -tln | grep -E ":(22|2222) "
EOF

set -euo pipefail

These are bash's "fail loudly" settings: -e stops at the first failing command,
-u treats an unset variable as an error, and pipefail makes a pipeline fail
if any stage fails, not just the last. Part 3 shows pipefail biting back,
too.

The user

  • adduser --disabled-password: the account has no password at all, so it can only be reached with a key. id ubuntu || … makes the line safe to run twice.
  • sudoers.d/90-ubuntu with NOPASSWD: ubuntu can run sudo without a password, which is what Ubuntu cloud images give their default user. It's a trade-off: if someone gets this account they get root. But a password-less account with a sudo password needs a password set somewhere, and that's a secret to manage. With key-only SSH, the key is the boundary. chmod 440 because sudo refuses sudoers files that others can write to.
  • install -d -m 700 / install -m 600: create .ssh and copy root's authorized_keys with the right owner and permissions in one step. DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive and --force-confold stop apt from opening an
interactive "a config file changed, which version do you want?" prompt in the
middle of a non-interactive SSH session. confold keeps the existing file.

Instead of editing /etc/ssh/sshd_config, we add a file in

first value it reads, so 10-hardening.conf beats the image's own

  • sshd -T (used later) prints the effective configuration after all files are merged. That's the only reliable way to know which value won.

Why ssh.socket and not just ssh

Since Ubuntu 24.04, sshd is socket-activated: systemd holds the listening
socket (ssh.socket) and starts sshd when a connection arrives. Which ports that
socket listens on is generated from sshd_config by a systemd generator, and

listens there. || true keeps the script going on releases that aren't

The script ends by printing what's listening. We got
0.0.0.0:22, 0.0.0.0:2222, [::]:22 and [::]:2222.

ufw: the host firewall

ufw ("uncomplicated firewall") is a front end for the kernel's netfilter
(nftables). Default deny incoming and allow outgoing, then open exactly
what's needed. 22 is allowed before ufw enable, otherwise enabling it would
cut the very session doing the enabling.

Docker bypasses ufw for published ports (see part 1), so ufw protects sshd and

defence in depth.

title: What Is the Most Important Quality of DevOps?
summary:
Imagine a busy restaurant kitchen on a Saturday night. The chefs have the best ovens money can buy, a perfectly organized pantry and a ticket system that prints orders in seconds. Yet if the chefs, the servers and the dishwashers do not talk to each other, plates still go out cold, orders get lost and everybody ends the night frustrated.

Software teams work the same way. You can buy the best tools in the market and still ship slowly and break things often. The thing that separates teams that succeed with DevOps from those that struggle is not a tool. It is a quality: shared ownership of the whole journey, from code to customer.

In this post, I’ll explain what that means, why it beats every other skill on the list, and how you can start practicing it this week.

The quick answer

The most important quality of DevOps is shared ownership, which grows out of honest collaboration. When developers, operations, QA and security all feel responsible for the result, not just their own step, the rest of DevOps becomes much easier.

What DevOps is trying to fix

In many companies, work used to move like a relay race with a dropped baton at every handoff. Developers wrote code and passed it on. Testers checked it and passed it on. Operations deployed it and kept it running. Each group had its own targets, and none of them owned the final outcome.

That setup creates familiar problems:

Releases that are slow because every handoff adds waiting time
Bugs that are found late, when they are expensive to fix
Outages followed by arguments about whose fault it was
Knowledge locked inside a few people’s heads

DevOps changes the question from “is my part done?” to “is the customer’s experience working?” That shift is a quality of mindset, not a feature of any product.

Why shared ownership matters more than tools

Tools follow habits, not the other way around. A new pipeline does not make people talk to each other. People who already work well together will build a good pipeline and keep it healthy.

Problems get found earlier. When developers care about how code behaves in production, they write more testable, more observable software. When operations people join planning, they flag risks before they become incidents.

Recovery gets faster. During an outage, nobody wastes time deciding who is responsible. Everyone knows the goal is the same: restore service, then learn from it.

People stay longer. Teams that trust each other and learn from mistakes without blame tend to be calmer and more engaged than teams that live in constant finger-pointing.

Signs your team already has it

Developers join on-call rotations or at least sit in on incident reviews
Operations engineers are involved while features are still being designed
After a failure, the first question is “what in our process allowed this?”
Documentation is written and updated by the people who do the work
Anyone can explain, in a few sentences, how a change travels to production

Signs it is missing

Tickets are thrown over the wall with no conversation
Only one person knows how a critical system works
Incident reports name a person instead of a cause
Developers say “that’s an ops problem” and operations says “that’s a dev problem”
Releases happen rarely because everyone is afraid of them

The supporting qualities

Shared ownership leads the way, but a few other qualities help it grow:

Curiosity and continuous learning. Cloud platforms and security threats change fast, so teams need to keep learning together.
An automation mindset. If a task is repetitive and error-prone, ask whether a script can do it. This frees people for more valuable work.
Clear communication. Good written updates, short runbooks and honest status messages are the everyday tools of collaboration.
Customer focus. Keep asking how a change will affect the people using your product.
Resilience. Things will break. Teams that stay calm and learn from failures improve faster.

How to start building it this week

Share one goal. Choose a metric developers and operations both care about, such as how quickly you can ship a safe change or how fast you recover from a problem.
Invite each other in. Ask operations to join a planning meeting. Ask a developer to shadow an on-call shift.
Run a blameless review. After the next incident, write down what happened, why it was possible and what you will change. Leave names out of the causes.
Write one runbook. Pick the system only one person understands and document it together.
Celebrate team wins. When a release goes smoothly, thank everyone who helped, not just whoever pressed the button.

None of this needs a budget or a new tool. It only needs a few honest conversations.

Mistakes to avoid

Believing that hiring a “DevOps engineer” alone creates DevOps
Rolling out new tools before agreeing on how people will work
Rewarding teams for conflicting goals, like speed for one and stability for the other
Using incident reviews to find someone to blame
Expecting culture to change in a month

Software teams work the same way. You can buy the best tools in the market and still ship slowly and break things often. The thing that separates teams that succeed with DevOps from those that struggle is not a tool. It is a quality: shared ownership of the whole journey, from code to customer.

In this post, I’ll explain what that means, why it beats every other skill on the list, and how you can start practicing it this week.

The quick answer

The most important quality of DevOps is shared ownership, which grows out of honest collaboration. When developers, operations, QA and security all feel responsible for the result, not just their own step, the rest of DevOps becomes much easier.

What DevOps is trying to fix

In many companies, work used to move like a relay race with a dropped baton at every handoff. Developers wrote code and passed it on. Testers checked it and passed it on. Operations deployed it and kept it running. Each group had its own targets, and none of them owned the final outcome.

That setup creates familiar problems:

Releases that are slow because every handoff adds waiting time
Bugs that are found late, when they are expensive to fix
Outages followed by arguments about whose fault it was
Knowledge locked inside a few people’s heads

DevOps changes the question from “is my part done?” to “is the customer’s experience working?” That shift is a quality of mindset, not a feature of any product.

Why shared ownership matters more than tools

Tools follow habits, not the other way around. A new pipeline does not make people talk to each other. People who already work well together will build a good pipeline and keep it healthy.

Problems get found earlier. When developers care about how code behaves in production, they write more testable, more observable software. When operations people join planning, they flag risks before they become incidents.

Recovery gets faster. During an outage, nobody wastes time deciding who is responsible. Everyone knows the goal is the same: restore service, then learn from it.

People stay longer. Teams that trust each other and learn from mistakes without blame tend to be calmer and more engaged than teams that live in constant finger-pointing.

Signs your team already has it

Developers join on-call rotations or at least sit in on incident reviews
Operations engineers are involved while features are still being designed
After a failure, the first question is “what in our process allowed this?”
Documentation is written and updated by the people who do the work
Anyone can explain, in a few sentences, how a change travels to production

Signs it is missing

Tickets are thrown over the wall with no conversation
Only one person knows how a critical system works
Incident reports name a person instead of a cause
Developers say “that’s an ops problem” and operations says “that’s a dev problem”
Releases happen rarely because everyone is afraid of them

The supporting qualities

Shared ownership leads the way, but a few other qualities help it grow:

Curiosity and continuous learning. Cloud platforms and security threats change fast, so teams need to keep learning together.
An automation mindset. If a task is repetitive and error-prone, ask whether a script can do it. This frees people for more valuable work.
Clear communication. Good written updates, short runbooks and honest status messages are the everyday tools of collaboration.
Customer focus. Keep asking how a change will affect the people using your product.
Resilience. Things will break. Teams that stay calm and learn from failures improve faster.

How to start building it this week

Share one goal. Choose a metric developers and operations both care about, such as how quickly you can ship a safe change or how fast you recover from a problem.
Invite each other in. Ask operations to join a planning meeting. Ask a developer to shadow an on-call shift.
Run a blameless review. After the next incident, write down what happened, why it was possible and what you will change. Leave names out of the causes.
Write one runbook. Pick the system only one person understands and document it together.
Celebrate team wins. When a release goes smoothly, thank everyone who helped, not just whoever pressed the button.

None of this needs a budget or a new tool. It only needs a few honest conversations.

Mistakes to avoid

Believing that hiring a “DevOps engineer” alone creates DevOps
Rolling out new tools before agreeing on how people will work
Rewarding teams for conflicting goals, like speed for one and stability for the other
Using incident reviews to find someone to blame
Expecting culture to change in a month

title: Understanding Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): A Practical Case Study of Amazon EC2
summary:
Introduction

Cloud computing has changed the way individuals and organizations access and manage computing resources. Traditionally, businesses had to purchase physical servers, storage devices and networking equipment before they could deploy applications. This required significant financial investment, technical expertise and continuous maintenance.

Today, cloud computing provides an alternative through different service models, one of which is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS).

This article explores the concept of IaaS, its features, benefits and challenges, using Amazon Web Services (AWS), particularly Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2), as a case study.

1. What Is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)?

Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) is a cloud computing model that provides virtualized computing resources such as servers, storage and networking over the internet.

Instead of purchasing physical servers and installing them in an office or organization, users can rent computing resources from a cloud service provider.

The cloud provider manages the physical infrastructure, including the servers, networking equipment and data centres, while customers manage their operating systems, applications and data.

For example, a business that wants to host a website does not necessarily need to purchase a physical server. It can rent a virtual server from an IaaS provider and use it to host its website.

3. Case Study: Amazon Web Services (AWS) EC2

Amazon Web Services (AWS) is one of the major cloud computing platforms. One of its infrastructure services is Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2).

Amazon EC2 provides virtual servers, known as instances, that allow individuals and organizations to run applications in the cloud.

Rather than purchasing physical servers, customers can launch EC2 instances, select their preferred operating systems and configure the resources required for their applications.

How Amazon EC2 Works

Consider a university that wants to develop an online course registration system.

Traditionally, the university might need to purchase physical servers, install operating systems, configure networking and provide storage facilities before deploying the application.

With Amazon EC2, the university can:

  1. Create an AWS account.
  2. Select an appropriate virtual server (EC2 instance).
  3. Choose an operating system, such as Linux or Windows Server.
  4. Configure the server's computing capacity, including memory and processing power.
  5. Configure network access and security settings.
  6. Install and deploy the university's course registration application.
  7. Increase or decrease computing resources as the number of users changes.

For instance, during course registration periods, many students may access the system simultaneously. The university can increase its computing capacity to accommodate the increased demand and reduce it when traffic decreases.

This demonstrates how IaaS provides flexibility and scalability.

Important Components of Amazon EC2

Some important components include:

  • EC2 Instances: Virtual servers used to run applications.
  • Amazon Machine Images (AMIs): Templates containing the operating system and other configurations required to launch instances.
  • Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS): Provides persistent storage for EC2 instances.
  • Security Groups: Act as virtual firewalls that control network traffic.
  • Instance Types: Determine the computing resources available, including CPU, memory and networking capacity.

4. Benefits of Using Amazon EC2 as an IaaS Solution

1. Reduced Hardware Costs

Organizations do not need to purchase expensive physical servers before deploying applications.

2. Scalability

Computing resources can be increased or decreased depending on application requirements.

3. Flexibility

Users can select different operating systems, server configurations and storage options.

4. Faster Deployment

Virtual servers can be launched without waiting for physical hardware to be purchased and installed.

5. Remote Management

Administrators can manage their cloud infrastructure through AWS management tools and interfaces.

5. Challenges and Limitations of IaaS

Despite its benefits, IaaS also has some limitations.

1. Security Responsibilities: Although the cloud provider manages the physical infrastructure, customers remain responsible for securing their operating systems, applications, access permissions and data.

2. Internet Dependency: Accessing cloud infrastructure generally requires a reliable internet connection.

3. Cost Management: Poor resource management can result in unexpected expenses, especially when unused resources continue running.

4. Technical Knowledge: Users need some knowledge of operating systems, networking, security and server administration to manage their infrastructure effectively.

6. Conclusion

Infrastructure as a Service has transformed how organizations obtain and manage computing resources. It reduces the need for physical infrastructure while providing flexibility, scalability and faster deployment of applications.

Amazon EC2 demonstrates how IaaS works by allowing users to rent virtual servers, configure their computing environments and deploy applications without purchasing physical servers.

For organizations such as universities, businesses and startups, IaaS provides an alternative to traditional infrastructure management.

As cloud computing continues to develop, understanding IaaS is important for students, developers and organizations interested in modern computing technologies.

References

  1. Amazon Web Services. (n.d.). What is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)?

  2. Amazon Web Services. (n.d.). What is Amazon EC2?

  3. Amazon Web Services. (n.d.). Amazon EC2 Documentation

title: Why Does Your API Work Locally but Fail in Production?
summary:
Every developer has experienced this frustrating situation.

Your API works perfectly on your local machine. You test the endpoints, connect the database, and everything looks good.

Then you deploy it to production.

Suddenly, things stop working.

You get a 500 error, database connection failures, missing environment variables, or unexpected behavior.

But why?

The answer is often that your local environment and production environment are not actually the same.

1. Environment variables are missing

One of the most common problems is missing or incorrectly configured environment variables.

Your local machine might have:

  • Database credentials
  • API keys
  • Secret keys
  • Third-party service URLs

But production may not have the same configuration.

For example:

DATABASE_URL=postgresql://localhost/mydb

This might work locally, but production requires a completely different database connection.

What to do:

  • Configure environment variables on the production server.
  • Never commit secrets to Git.
  • Validate required configuration when the application starts.

2. Database differences

Your local database might contain test data, while production has real data and different permissions.

Common problems include:

  • Missing database migrations
  • Different database versions
  • Incorrect user permissions
  • Missing indexes or constraints
  • Different timezone settings

Before deployment, make sure your database schema is up to date.

3. Different runtime versions

Your application might run on Node.js 22 locally but Node.js 18 in production.

The same problem can happen with PHP, Python, database engines, and other dependencies.

Different versions can introduce compatibility problems.

A good practice: define and document the runtime versions your application requires.

4. CORS and server configuration

An API can work perfectly when called from localhost but fail when accessed through your production frontend.

Possible reasons include:

  • Incorrect CORS configuration
  • HTTPS and HTTP mismatches
  • Reverse proxy configuration
  • Incorrect request size limits
  • Missing headers

Check the browser's Network tab and your server logs instead of guessing.

5. Production errors are harder to debug

Locally, developers often see detailed error messages.

In production, errors may be hidden from the client for security reasons.

That is good practice, but your server should still record useful diagnostic information.

Log:

  • Error messages
  • Request IDs
  • Relevant timestamps
  • Failed operations
  • Stack traces in protected server logs

Never expose passwords, access tokens, or sensitive user data in logs.

A simple pre-deployment checklist

Before deploying an API, check:

  • [ ] Environment variables are configured.
  • [ ] Database migrations have been applied.
  • [ ] Runtime and dependency versions are compatible.
  • [ ] CORS and HTTPS settings are correct.
  • [ ] Health-check endpoint is working.
  • [ ] Server-side error logging is enabled.
  • [ ] Important API endpoints have been tested.

Final Thoughts

An API working locally does not guarantee that it will work in production.

The production environment has different configurations, infrastructure, permissions, and real-world traffic.

Instead of treating deployment as the final step, treat production readiness as part of development from the beginning.

Question for developers: What is the most frustrating production-only bug you have ever faced?

Share your experience in the comments. It might help another developer avoid the same problem.

title: Moving a production API to Hetzner, part 1: choosing and creating the server
summary:
Series: Part 1: choosing and creating the server · Part 2: hardening and configuring it · Part 3: migrating data and cutting over

I recently moved a small production API from one VPS provider to Hetzner Cloud.
The stack is ordinary: a Rust web server, PostgreSQL, Valkey (the open-source
Redis fork), and Caddy as the TLS-terminating reverse proxy, all under Docker
Compose. Encrypted blobs live in S3-compatible object storage, which doesn't
move at all.

These posts are both the record of what I did and a tutorial. Each step comes
with the command, what it does, and why it works that way, because
most migration guides give the commands and skip the reasons, and the reasons
are what you need when something goes wrong. Plenty did go wrong, and I've left
those parts in.

Throughout, the addresses are placeholders from the documentation ranges reserved for examples (RFC 5737 and RFC 3849):

Placeholder Means
203.0.113.10 the old server
198.51.100.20 the new Hetzner server
2001:db8:1234:5678::/64 the new server's IPv6 range
api.example.com the API's domain
old-box, new-box SSH aliases for the two servers (set up in part 2)

What we are moving

Only Caddy publishes ports to the outside world. Everything else talks over
Docker's private network. That detail comes back several times, because it
decides what the firewall has to allow and what the migration has to copy.

1. Picking a server type

The three families

When you click Add Server, the Type step splits the catalogue into
Shared Resources (two families) and Dedicated Resources (one):

Family Series CPU Hetzner's own pitch Who it's for
Cost-Optimized (shared) CX (x86) and CAX (Arm64) shared Intel/AMD, older hardware generations "cost-efficient… with limited availability" small production services, side projects. Cheapest per GB of RAM
Regular Performance (shared) CPX shared AMD, newer hardware generations "best price/performance" the same jobs with faster, more consistent CPU
General Purpose (dedicated) CCX dedicated AMD vCPUs, latest hardware "predictable performance, critical production" sustained CPU load: builds, busy databases

Here is each family as the console showed it in Helsinki on the day I
created the server (October 2026, USD per month, excluding VAT):

Cost-Optimized. CX23 is 2 vCPU, 4 GB, 40 GB for $6.49. Note that every row is greyed out: at that moment none of them could be ordered in Helsinki. The
summary on the right still says CPX22 because a greyed row can't be selected.

Regular Performance. CPX22 has the same 2 vCPU and 4 GB as CX23 (with 80 GB of disk) for $22.99, more than three times the price.

General Purpose. Dedicated cores start at CCX13 (2 vCPU, 8 GB) for $50.49.

The panel on the right shows one cost that's easy to miss: a public IPv4 is billed on top of the server, $0.60/month.

Cost-Optimized also offers Arm64 (Ampere), which is often the best value of all. I couldn't use it: our container image is built for amd64 only.

Check your image's architecture before choosing Arm. docker manifest inspect lists the platforms it was built for.

"Shared" means your virtual CPU is a time slice of a physical core that other
customers' VMs use too. Most of the time you get the whole slice. When a
neighbour is busy you may get less, which is called CPU steal (shown as st
in top). For an API that idles most of the day that's fine; for a CI runner,
it isn't. Dedicated vCPUs are reserved for you, which is what the large price
jump buys.

How big does it have to be?

Measure before you buy. On the old server, docker stats --no-stream and
free -h showed the entire stack using about 1 GB. On the fresh Hetzner box,
Ubuntu itself sat at about 500 MB used after boot.

Option (Helsinki, October 2026) vCPU / RAM / disk Monthly + IPv4 Verdict
CPX02 (Regular Performance) 1 / 1 GB / 20 GB $7.49 + $0.60 too small: Postgres, Valkey, the server and Caddy together would spill into swap
CPX12 (Regular Performance) 1 / 2 GB / 40 GB $13.49 + $0.60 tight on RAM, and double CX23's price
CX23 (Cost-Optimized) 2 / 4 GB / 40 GB $6.49 + $0.60 chosen: 4× headroom on RAM, the cheapest option that fits
CPX22 (Regular Performance) 2 / 4 GB / 80 GB $22.99 + $0.60 the fallback if CX23 stays unavailable
CCX13 (General Purpose) 2 dedicated / 8 GB / 80 GB $50.49 + $0.60 far more than an idle API needs

Prices change; take today's from the console, not from this table.

"Limited availability" is real

Cost-Optimized types carry a limited availability label, and it means it. When
I first configured the server, CX23 in Helsinki was available. A few minutes later,
when I came back to click Create, the whole CX row set was greyed out: not available (the first screenshot above)..

Hetzner allocates these types from a pool of hosts per location. When a
location's pool is full, the type disappears there until capacity frees up.
Your options:

  1. Change the location. Nuremberg (nbg1) and Falkenstein (fsn1) in Germany and Helsinki (hel1) in Finland are all in the eu-central network zone, with similar latency to most of Europe. The type is often in stock at one of the others.
  2. Wait and retry. Capacity comes and goes during the day. My CX23 in Helsinki came back later.
  3. Pick the next family up (CPX), if you can't wait and the price is acceptable.

A consequence I didn't expect: once you hold a scarce server type, deleting the
server to fix a mistake is risky. You may not get another one. That shaped
part 2, where I fixed a setup mistake on the running server instead of
recreating it.

Location and image

  • Location: as close as possible to your users and to your object storage. My storage is a global-anycast S3 provider, so any EU location was fine.
  • Image: Ubuntu 26.04 LTS. "LTS" means five years of security updates, which is what you want on a server you'd rather not rebuild. 24.04 LTS would have been equally good.

2. SSH keys: how you'll get in

What a key pair is

An SSH key pair is two halves of one mathematical object:

  • the private key (~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519) stays on your laptop and never leaves it;
  • the public key (~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519.pub) goes on every server you want to log in to, in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys.

The server never learns your private key. At login it asks your SSH client to
sign a value that is unique to this connection. Your client signs it with the
private key, and the server checks the signature against the public key it has
on file. A valid signature proves you hold the private key without the key ever
crossing the network.

Notice there are two key pairs in play:

Key Belongs to Proves Stored where
host key the server "I really am 198.51.100.20, not an impostor" server: /etc/ssh/ssh_host_*; your laptop remembers it in ~/.ssh/known_hosts
user key you "I'm allowed to log in as ubuntu" laptop: private key; server: authorized_keys

The first time you connect, SSH shows the host key's fingerprint and asks
whether to trust it. This is called TOFU: trust on first use. If the host key
later changes, for example because you rebuilt the server, SSH refuses to connect
and warns about a possible man-in-the-middle. That's correct behaviour. After a
deliberate rebuild, remove the old entry with ssh-keygen -R .

Creating the key 

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519 -C hetzner-api
  • -t ed25519: a modern elliptic-curve key. It's short (one line), fast, and has no weak-parameter choices to get wrong, unlike older RSA keys.
  • -f: the file name. A separate key per provider means losing or rotating one doesn't touch the others.
  • -C: a comment, just a label so you can recognise the key in authorized_keys later.

It asks for a passphrase. Use one: it encrypts the private key on disk, and
ssh-agent remembers it for your session, so you type it once.

Print the public half and paste it into Hetzner → Security → SSH keys → Add
SSH key:

cat ~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519.pub

When you pick this key on the create screen, Hetzner writes it into the new
server's /root/.ssh/authorized_keys, and, as a side effect, does not set a
root password at all. Remember that; it matters in part 2.

3. Primary IPs: an address that outlives the server

What a Primary IP is

In Hetzner Cloud, a server's public address is a separate resource called a
Primary IP. It's created along with the server and attached to it, but it has
a life of its own:

  • IPv4: one address, billed separately (about $0.60/month), because the world has run out of IPv4.
  • IPv6: a whole /64 network, free. That's 2⁶⁴ addresses; the server uses the first one by convention (2001:db8:1234:5678::1).

Why "auto delete" matters

Each Primary IP has an auto delete switch. On, the address is released when
the server is deleted, and you'll probably never get it back. Off, the address
stays in your project, unattached, ready to assign to a replacement server.

Why you want it off for production:

  • DNS points at it. A new address means a DNS change, and DNS changes take a while to reach everyone (part 3 explains TTLs).
  • Other services may allowlist it. Object-storage tokens, database firewalls and payment-provider webhook settings sometimes filter by source IP.
  • It's your escape hatch. If the server breaks beyond repair, you can delete it and create a new one with the same address.

Turn it off in IPs → (the IPv4) → ⋯. If the menu offers "Enable Auto
Delete", it's already off.

I didn't add an IPv6 (AAAA) DNS record. The old server had none, so the
migration changes as little as possible. That can come later.

4. The Cloud Firewall: the perimeter outside your VM

Two places a firewall can sit

A Hetzner Cloud Firewall filters traffic in Hetzner's network, before it
reaches your VM. A host firewall like ufw filters it inside the VM.

The difference matters because of Docker. When a container publishes a port
(ports: ["443:443"]), Docker writes its own NAT rules that send the packet to
the container before it reaches the chain ufw controls. So ufw deny 443
does not block a published Docker port, and plenty of people have exposed a
database to the internet this way while ufw status said everything was closed.

The Cloud Firewall can't be bypassed from inside the VM, so it is the real
perimeter. ufw (set up in part 2) is a second layer for anything that isn't
Docker.

Stateful filtering, in one paragraph

Both firewalls are stateful: they track connections. You write rules for
new incoming connections only. Replies to connections your server opened (to
download packages, call an API, fetch a certificate) are recognised as part of
an existing connection and let back in automatically. That's why the rule set

Series: Part 1: choosing and creating the server · Part 2: hardening and configuring it · Part 3: migrating data and cutting over

I recently moved a small production API from one VPS provider to Hetzner Cloud.
The stack is ordinary: a Rust web server, PostgreSQL, Valkey (the open-source
Redis fork), and Caddy as the TLS-terminating reverse proxy, all under Docker
Compose. Encrypted blobs live in S3-compatible object storage, which doesn't
move at all.

These posts are both the record of what I did and a tutorial. Each step comes
with the command, what it does, and why it works that way, because
most migration guides give the commands and skip the reasons, and the reasons
are what you need when something goes wrong. Plenty did go wrong, and I've left
those parts in.

Throughout, the addresses are placeholders from the documentation ranges reserved for examples (RFC 5737 and RFC 3849):

Placeholder Means
203.0.113.10 the old server
198.51.100.20 the new Hetzner server
2001:db8:1234:5678::/64 the new server's IPv6 range
api.example.com the API's domain
old-box, new-box SSH aliases for the two servers (set up in part 2)

What we are moving

Only Caddy publishes ports to the outside world. Everything else talks over

decides what the firewall has to allow and what the migration has to copy.

1. Picking a server type

The three families

When you click Add Server, the Type step splits the catalogue into
Shared Resources (two families) and Dedicated Resources (one):

Family Series CPU Hetzner's own pitch Who it's for
Cost-Optimized (shared) CX (x86) and CAX (Arm64) shared Intel/AMD, older hardware generations "cost-efficient… with limited availability" small production services, side projects. Cheapest per GB of RAM
Regular Performance (shared) CPX shared AMD, newer hardware generations "best price/performance" the same jobs with faster, more consistent CPU
General Purpose (dedicated) CCX dedicated AMD vCPUs, latest hardware "predictable performance, critical production" sustained CPU load: builds, busy databases
