created the server (October 2026, USD per month, excluding VAT):

Cost-Optimized. CX23 is 2 vCPU, 4 GB, 40 GB for $6.49. Note that every row is greyed out: at that moment none of them could be ordered in Helsinki. The
summary on the right still says CPX22 because a greyed row can't be selected.

Regular Performance. CPX22 has the same 2 vCPU and 4 GB as CX23 (with 80 GB of disk) for $22.99, more than three times the price.

General Purpose. Dedicated cores start at CCX13 (2 vCPU, 8 GB) for $50.49.

Cost-Optimized also offers Arm64 (Ampere), which is often the best value of all. I couldn't use it: our container image is built for amd64 only.

"Shared" means your virtual CPU is a time slice of a physical core that other
customers' VMs use too. Most of the time you get the whole slice. When a
neighbour is busy you may get less, which is called CPU steal (shown as st

CPX02 (Regular Performance) 1 / 1 GB / 20 GB $7.49 + $0.60 too small: Postgres, Valkey, the server and Caddy together would spill into swap
CPX12 (Regular Performance) 1 / 2 GB / 40 GB $13.49 + $0.60 tight on RAM, and double CX23's price

CPX22 (Regular Performance) 2 / 4 GB / 80 GB $22.99 + $0.60 the fallback if CX23 stays unavailable
CCX13 (General Purpose) 2 dedicated / 8 GB / 80 GB $50.49 + $0.60 far more than an idle API needs

Prices change; take today's from the console, not from this table.

location's pool is full, the type disappears there until capacity frees up.

  1. Change the location. Nuremberg (nbg1) and Falkenstein (fsn1) in Germany and Helsinki (hel1) in Finland are all in the eu-central network zone, with similar latency to most of Europe. The type is often in stock at one of the others.

What a key pair is

An SSH key pair is two halves of one mathematical object:

  • the private key (~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519) stays on your laptop and never leaves it;

sign a value that is unique to this connection. Your client signs it with the
private key, and the server checks the signature against the public key it has
on file. A valid signature proves you hold the private key without the key ever

What a Primary IP is

In Hetzner Cloud, a server's public address is a separate resource called a

  • IPv4: one address, billed separately (about $0.60/month), because the world has run out of IPv4.

Each Primary IP has an auto delete switch. On, the address is released when
the server is deleted, and you'll probably never get it back. Off, the address
stays in your project, unattached, ready to assign to a replacement server.

Why you want it off for production:

  • DNS points at it. A new address means a DNS change, and DNS changes take a while to reach everyone (part 3 explains TTLs).
  • Other services may allowlist it. Object-storage tokens, database firewalls and payment-provider webhook settings sometimes filter by source IP.
  • It's your escape hatch. If the server breaks beyond repair, you can delete it and create a new one with the same address.

I didn't add an IPv6 (AAAA) DNS record. The old server had none, so the

Two places a firewall can sit

A Hetzner Cloud Firewall filters traffic in Hetzner's network, before it

The difference matters because of Docker. When a container publishes a port

title: WARDEN: Hunting the Ghost in the Machine with an AI-Powered Self-Healing DevOps Agent
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

WARDEN is an AI-powered self-healing DevOps agent that detects service failures, investigates their root causes, proposes safe remediation actions, and verifies whether the system has actually recovered.

Every production system has its ghosts.

A sudden traffic spike. An exhausted connection pool. Unexpected HTTP 503 errors. A service that appears healthy but silently struggles under concurrent load.

These failures can be difficult to diagnose. Engineers often spend valuable time switching between logs, metrics, configuration files, and monitoring dashboards.

I wanted to explore a different approach:

What if an AI agent could investigate incidents and help resolve them while keeping safety and human approval at the center?

That idea became WARDEN.

WARDEN follows a four-stage incident response workflow:

Detect → Diagnose → Remediate → Verify

Key Features

  • Incident Detection: Monitors service health, telemetry, logs, latency, and HTTP failure rates.
  • AI-Powered Diagnosis: Analyzes incident information and identifies potential root causes.
  • Safe Remediation: Restricts proposed actions to a predefined allowlist with strict parameter boundaries.
  • Human-in-the-Loop Approval: Requires operator authorization before applying configuration changes.
  • Empirical Recovery Verification: Uses concurrent HTTP requests to determine whether the service has genuinely recovered.
  • Audit Trail: Maintains structured records of incident and remediation events.

The Ghost in the Machine

For the demonstration, WARDEN manages a FastAPI-based payment-service simulator.

I can deliberately introduce connection-pool exhaustion, causing the service to return HTTP 503 errors under concurrent traffic.

WARDEN then:

  1. Detects the service degradation.
  2. Analyzes metrics and logs to identify connection-pool starvation.
  3. Proposes an increase to the connection-pool limit.
  4. Waits for explicit operator approval.
  5. Applies the permitted configuration change.
  6. Runs another concurrent HTTP verification to measure recovery.

The important part is that WARDEN does not simply announce that an incident is fixed because a configuration changed.

It verifies recovery using actual HTTP responses.

Demo

Watch WARDEN in action:

▶️ Watch the WARDEN Project Demo on YouTube

The demonstration showcases the project's incident-response workflow and recovery capabilities.

Code

The project is open source and available on GitHub:

WARDEN - AI-Powered Self-Healing DevOps Agent

Technology Stack

  • Python
  • FastAPI
  • Streamlit
  • Nebius Token Factory
  • OpenAI-compatible SDK
  • Pydantic
  • HTTPX
  • Pytest
  • Tavily (optional technical research integration)

Project Architecture 

WARDEN/
│
├── warden/
│   ├── app.py
│   ├── payment_service.py
│   ├── agent.py
│   ├── nebius_client.py
│   ├── tavily_client.py
│   ├── verifier.py
│   ├── remediation.py
│   ├── schemas.py
│   └── audit.py
│
├── tests/
├── requirements.txt
├── pytest.ini
└── README.md

The repository includes automated tests for service behavior, remediation safety, agent output validation, and empirical recovery verification.

How I Built It

WARDEN combines an AI reasoning layer with deterministic execution controls.

1. AI Reasoning

The agent architecture supports open-weight models through Nebius Token Factory's OpenAI-compatible API.

The documented model configurations include:

  • Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct for lower-latency diagnostic tasks.
  • Meta-Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct for more complex incident analysis.
  • DeepSeek-R1 as an alternative reasoning model configuration.

The architecture separates fast triage from deeper reasoning so that model selection can match the complexity of an incident.

A deterministic Demo Mode is also available, allowing the incident-response workflow to operate without API credentials.

2. Safety Before Automation

Giving an AI agent unrestricted access to production infrastructure would introduce serious operational risks.

WARDEN takes a constrained approach.

The agent cannot execute arbitrary shell commands, Python code, SQL, or unrestricted operations.

Instead, remediation is limited to explicitly permitted actions:

  • increase_pool_limit
  • reset_service_config
  • no_op

Numeric boundaries are enforced through deterministic validation, and configuration changes require explicit operator approval.

3. Real Recovery Verification

WARDEN uses HTTPX and asynchronous requests to evaluate service behavior under concurrent load.

It measures actual HTTP responses and performance indicators instead of trusting the agent's claims.

A proposed fix is not the same thing as a verified recovery.

4. Testing

The project includes 18 automated tests covering:

  • Service health and concurrency behavior.
  • HTTP 503 responses under overload.
  • Administrative authentication.
  • Remediation allowlists and parameter boundaries.
  • Human approval enforcement.
  • Structured diagnostic validation.
  • Recovery verification.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open innovation matters because infrastructure automation should not depend on a single closed model or an opaque decision-making system.

Using open-weight model options through an inference platform such as Nebius Token Factory provides flexibility in model selection while allowing developers to retain control over the surrounding application architecture.

For WARDEN, the reasoning model is only one component of the system.

The application also contains independently testable safety validators, structured schemas, deterministic remediation rules, and recovery verification.

This separation makes it possible to experiment with different models without giving them unrestricted control over infrastructure operations.

Open innovation also makes it easier for developers to inspect, adapt, test, and extend the system according to their own operational requirements.

My Agent Session

WARDEN's incident lifecycle can be demonstrated through its dashboard:

Incident → Diagnosis → Approval → Remediation → Verification

The Spirit of It

The most interesting part of building WARDEN was realizing that an AI agent should not be judged only by how intelligently it explains a problem.

It should also be judged by what happens after its recommendation.

Does the service actually recover?

Can the action be trusted?

Can an engineer understand what changed?

And can the system prove that the incident is resolved?

I wanted to build something that goes beyond an AI chatbot suggesting commands.

WARDEN represents an approach where AI reasoning works together with deterministic safety, human oversight, and measurable outcomes.

The ghost in the machine might be invisible, but its impact is measurable.

WARDEN: Find the failure. Understand the cause. Fix it safely. Prove the recovery.

title: Bounding CI Cost Without Weakening Trust in Keploy Pull Requests
summary:
Bounding CI Cost Without Weakening Trust in Keploy Pull Requests

It's 2:47 AM and your GitHub Actions budget notification fires: 90% consumed with eleven days left in the billing cycle. You check the console and find forty-three overlapping CI runs—someone pushed a quick typo fix eight times in fifteen minutes, and every push triggered a full matrix build with no cancellation policy. Each job compiles Go packages, runs the test suite, exercises privileged recording infrastructure, and uploads artifacts. None of them will finish before the next push arrives and starts the cycle again.

That incident reveals two independent failures: there was no concept of superseded work, and different trust boundaries were collapsed into a single expensive job. Fixing only one leaves the other intact. For keploy/keploy adoption, where production-sandbox testing involves compiling Go, testing application behavior, and exercising privileged recording or replay infrastructure, those boundaries matter. Putting them in one oversized workflow makes cancellation expensive and failures difficult to interpret.

The configuration below is an adoption baseline—not a claim about Keploy's current workflows or measured coverage. It assumes a root Go module and requires validation against the repository's actual toolchain and test prerequisites before becoming a required check.

The Failure Is Usually Multiplication

Consider a representative scenario: a maintainer adds a third-party reporting action by mutable tag. Later, that tag resolves to compromised code. Meanwhile, contributors repeatedly push fixes, creating overlapping matrix runs with no concurrency policy.

These failures compound. The compromised action executes wherever it is referenced; redundant runs multiply both exposure and runner consumption. A workflow timeout limits each job, but it does not stop twenty obsolete jobs from starting.

The root causes are independent: dependency identity was mutable, and scheduling had no concept of superseded work. For Keploy adoption, I separate the architecture into three layers: an unprivileged pull-request gate, isolated Linux integration execution, and trusted publishing. Only the first belongs below. Recording, replay, privileged networking, production-derived artifacts, and release credentials stay outside this gate.

One Workflow, With an Embedded Validation Script

Save this as .github/workflows/pr-go.yml. The single configuration creates a Bash script so local validation and CI policy have an explicit, auditable implementation. Once adopted, move that script into a tracked file without changing its behavior.

name: PR Go gate

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: go-${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.event.pull_request.number || github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  validate:
    name: Go / ${{ matrix.os }}
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    timeout-minutes: 20
    strategy:
      fail-fast: true
      max-parallel: 2
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-22.04, ubuntu-24.04]
    env:
      MIN_COVERAGE: "60"

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683 # v4.2.2
        with:
          persist-credentials: false

      - uses: actions/setup-go@0a12ed9d6a96ab950c8f026ed9f722fe0da7ef32 # v5
        with:
          go-version-file: go.mod
          cache: false

      - name: Locate Go caches
        id: paths
        shell: bash
        run: |
          echo "mod=$(go env GOMODCACHE)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "build=$(go env GOCACHE)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "version=$(go env GOVERSION)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - uses: actions/cache@0400d5f644dc74513175e3cd8d07132dd4860809 # v4.2.4
        with:
          path: |
            ${{ steps.paths.outputs.mod }}
            ${{ steps.paths.outputs.build }}
          key: go-${{ runner.os }}-${{ runner.arch }}-${{ matrix.os }}-${{ steps.paths.outputs.version }}-${{ hashFiles('go.sum') }}

      - name: Validate source
        shell: bash
        run: |
          cat > "$RUNNER_TEMP/validate.sh" <<'BASH'
          #!/usr/bin/env bash
          set -euo pipefail
          mapfile -d '' files < <(git ls-files -z '*.go')
          if ((${#files[@]})); then
            unformatted="$(gofmt -l "${files[@]}")"
            if [[ -n "$unformatted" ]]; then
              printf 'Unformatted Go files:\n%s\n' "$unformatted"
              exit 1
            fi
          fi
          go mod download
          go mod verify
          go vet ./...
          go build ./...
          go test -race -count=1 -timeout=8m \
            -covermode=atomic -coverprofile=coverage.out ./...
          actual="$(go tool cover -func=coverage.out |
            awk '$1 == "total:" {gsub(/%/, "", $3); print $3}')"
          awk -v actual="$actual" -v minimum="$MIN_COVERAGE" '
            BEGIN {
              printf "Coverage: %s%%; required: %s%%\n", actual, minimum
              exit !(actual != "" && actual + 0 >= minimum + 0)
            }'
          BASH
          bash "$RUNNER_TEMP/validate.sh"

What This Boundary Actually Guarantees

The matrix checks two Linux environments without inventing an unsupported Go-version range; go.mod supplies the toolchain request. Confirm that both runner images support the repository's required native libraries. Go's toolchain selection can still download a newer toolchain requested by the module.

The script enforces formatting, static analysis, compilation with type checking, race-enabled tests, and a coverage floor. Sixty percent is an example policy, not Keploy's reported coverage. Measure the baseline before enabling branch protection. Package-default coverage also does not prove that replay paths or failure recovery received meaningful exercise.

Tests requiring privileges or external services will fail here. Classify those tests explicitly using the repository's supported package selection or build tags; do not quietly replace the command with a narrower suite and retain a misleading "full validation" label.

The Trade-Offs Worth Keeping

Exact action SHAs prevent a moving tag from silently changing execution. They do not certify the pinned code or freeze every dependency it downloads. Review updates, retain version comments for maintainability, and audit transitive execution separately.

The cache key includes the operating system, architecture, runner image, Go version, and dependency checksum file. Omitting broad restore prefixes sacrifices some cache hits for simpler provenance. Cache entries accelerate work; checksum verification and successful validation remain necessary.

Concurrency cancellation keeps only the newest run for a pull request. max-parallel bounds this matrix, not the entire repository's runner consumption. Separate pull requests still run concurrently, and cancellation is not instantaneous. Organization-level budgets and runner limits remain necessary.

Finally, keep publishing out of this workflow. Read-only permissions and disabled persisted Git credentials reduce exposure, but pull-request tests still execute contributor-controlled code. Avoid pull_request_target for that execution path, and never assume a self-hosted runner is safe simply because the token is read-only.

For Keploy, this boundary preserves a useful distinction: cheap source feedback can be aggressive and disposable; privileged integration evidence must be isolated and deliberate.

The Hardest Trade-Off

The configuration above makes one deliberate sacrifice: it prefers cache simplicity over hit rate. A more aggressive restore strategy could reuse module caches across Go version bumps or checksum updates, improving cold-start latency at the cost of provenance clarity. That trade-off is testable—measure your cache hit rate and typical download overhead, then decide whether the complexity is worth the seconds saved.

What's your tolerance for cache complexity versus build speed? Have you seen a setup where aggressive fallback keys caused more confusion than they prevented, or the opposite—where conservative caching created unnecessary pain during dependency churn?

title: The largest robbery in cryptocurrency history with the theft of $5,9 billion from Binance
summary:
Binance reported a security incident affecting ~$6.3 billion in assets, surpassing previous heists.

Initial findings suggest a compromised DevOps engineer laptop allowed access to a service container for unauthorized withdrawals, with no evidence of private key leaks.

According to the company, initial investigation indicates that an engineer's laptop was compromised, allowing someone to gain access to a service system and send unauthorized withdrawal commands.

Binance clarified that there is no indication that digital wallet keys were leaked. At the same time, it announced that it will fully cover all losses from its security fund and its own funds.

How much money has been frozen?

So far, nearly $3 billion of affected assets have been frozen directly on the networks.

title: Treating Dev, Staging and Production as Real Git Branches
summary:
It is 2 a.m. and an engineer at an Austin fintech is staring at a production alert, trying to answer a question that should be trivial: what code is actually running right now? The repo says one thing. The deploy log says another. Someone merged a hotfix directly to a release branch three weeks ago and nobody back-ported it to main. This is not a rare failure mode — it is the default state of most pipelines that treat 'environment' as a label instead of a fact.

The cost of that ambiguity is not abstract. ITIC's commonly cited figure puts the median cost of production downtime for large enterprises at roughly $9,000 per minute. Every minute spent reconciling what-is-live-versus-what-is-committed is a minute charged at that rate, and it is almost always a senior engineer's time — the one person who remembers how the deploy scripts actually work.

Where promotion usually breaks

Most teams do not lack a concept of dev, staging and production. They lack a single source of truth for what is in each one. Config flags, environment variables, separate CI jobs per stage, manual 'sync this branch to that server' steps — each is a point where the running system can diverge silently from version control. When an incident report comes in, the first job is archaeology, not diagnosis.

This gets worse under real staffing constraints. The tech-talent shortage is not a North American curiosity — skills-gap figures from the Gulf region sit near 90% of organizations reporting a gap, and in Europe roughly 57% of firms say they cannot find qualified developers to hire. Austin, Toronto and New York teams are competing in the same global pool for the same scarce senior engineers, which means the person who understands your deploy quirks is also the person you can least afford to pull into firefighting.

The mechanism: environments as branches, promotion as a pull request

Corporate AI 365 removes the ambiguity by making the environment literally a git ref. Dev, staging and production are branches in your own repository — connected through GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket or Azure DevOps — and a change does not 'go to production' through a side channel. It moves as a pull request from one branch to the next, through Developer, QA, approval and production gates, each one a real diff with a real reviewer and a real merge commit.

That has a direct consequence for incident response. When the AI reads your codebase and scripted schema and diagnoses a problem down to a file, class or line — with a confidence score and a proposed fix — that fix is proposed as a branch off dev and travels the same governed path as any human-authored change. There is no separate hotfix lane outside git history. If you need to roll back a release, you are reverting a merge commit, not guessing which server got which script.

Every gate is tied to one of 41 composable permissions and your org's real hierarchy, so 'who approved this' and 'what did QA actually look at' are questions answered by the commit log, not by someone's memory of a Slack thread. And because your CI confirms the result, 'it shipped' is a build status, not an assertion.

What the AI does not touch

None of this requires the AI to see anything it should not. Corporate AI 365 never hosts your code and never connects to a live database. It reasons over source code and a scripted schema export you control — never a connection string, never live rows. When a diagnosis genuinely needs live data to confirm, the AI writes a read-only query and hands it to your own developer to run; the result never comes back to us. That boundary is what ends a security review early, and we are not going to soften it for convenience.

The diagnosis itself is reproducible — cached against a hash of the issue text, the code snapshot and the model used — so the same report produces the same root cause and the same proposed fix each time. That matters specifically because of the branch-based pipeline: an approval gate is only meaningful if the thing being approved is stable, not a different answer on every re-run.

The practical effect for a lean North American team is that production support stops depending entirely on your scarcest senior engineer. Anyone in the company — support, ops, a department head who isn't a developer — can file a plain-language report through the Employee console. The AI gets you to a confident, file-level starting point. QA and an approver, both human, still decide what merges. You are not removing judgment from the pipeline; you are removing the hours of archaeology that used to precede it.

There is no separate hotfix lane outside git history. If you need to roll back a release, you are reverting a merge commit, not guessing which server got which script.

Every gate is tied to one of 41 composable permissions and your org's real hierarchy, so 'who approved this' and 'what did QA actually look at' are questions answered by the commit log, not by someone's memory of a Slack thread. And because your CI confirms the result, 'it shipped' is a build status, not an assertion.

What the AI does not touch

None of this requires the AI to see anything it should not. Corporate AI 365 never hosts your code and never connects to a live database. It reasons over source code and a scripted schema export you control — never a connection string, never live rows. When a diagnosis genuinely needs live data to confirm, the AI writes a read-only query and hands it to your own developer to run; the result never comes back to us. That boundary is what ends a security review early, and we are not going to soften it for convenience.

The diagnosis itself is reproducible — cached against a hash of the issue text, the code snapshot and the model used — so the same report produces the same root cause and the same proposed fix each time. That matters specifically because of the branch-based pipeline: an approval gate is only meaningful if the thing being approved is stable, not a different answer on every re-run.

The practical effect for a lean North American team is that production support stops depending entirely on your scarcest senior engineer. Anyone in the company — support, ops, a department head who isn't a developer — can file a plain-language report through the Employee console. The AI gets you to a confident, file-level starting point. QA and an approver, both human, still decide what merges. You are not removing judgment from the pipeline; you are removing the hours of archaeology that used to precede it.

title: Fast Isn't Free
summary:
A team picks a workflow tool. It runs well in testing, so they ship it.

A year later, traffic is up. The bill is up even more.

Nobody planned for that, because nobody asked the right question at the start. Not "how fast is it?" but "what will it cost when we're ten times bigger?"

Turn speed into daily volume

Throughput numbers are usually quoted per second, which makes them hard to feel. A quick conversion helps: multiply transactions per second by 86,400, the number of seconds in a day.

  • 1,000 per second is about 86 million a day
  • 10,000 per second is about 864 million a day

Now compare that with what you really expect. A lot of teams find they need far less than they feared. Others find they need a lot more than they planned for. Either way, you can't judge a tool until you know your own number.

Watch how the cost grows

A tool can be fine at small volume and painful at large volume. Here's an illustration. Spending $20,000 a year for a few thousand transactions per second might be reasonable. If handling a bigger load pushed that to $200,000, the math changes. Those are example figures, not anyone's price list, but the shape is real: what matters is whether cost rises in step with traffic or faster.

Simple workflows that run at low volume can live happily with a modest setup. Complex, high-volume ones can't. And a setup that's fast but very expensive tends to be dropped once the bill gets attention.

When latency is the whole point

Some use cases don't give you time to wait. Payment processing, IoT data pipelines and AI-driven workflows are all situations where slow responses or low throughput cause real problems for users. If yours looks like that, test under load before you commit, not after.

What to ask before you choose

  • How many transactions per second can one instance sustain, and what did that test look like?
  • What happens when you need more? Do you add instances, and how does the price change?
  • Does the number come from a workflow like yours, or a simple one-step example?
  • What does it cost at your expected volume, and at ten times that?

Those four questions tell you more than any single benchmark.

For reference, Unmeshed reports up to 10,000 transactions per second on a single instance, which works out to nearly a billion a day, and says larger loads are handled by adding instances to the cluster. As with any vendor's numbers, test it against your own workflows. You can try Unmeshed and see how it behaves with yours.
